entries.searchText: Rate of photosynthesis Explain limiting factors and analyse a light-intensity investigation. ,must:['Limiting factors include light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature and chlorophyll.','A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply for the current conditions.'],practical:'Required Practical 6: vary light intensity or lamp distance, measure oxygen production over time, control temperature/CO₂/plant material/time, repeat and calculate a mean.',extension:'Using 1/d² as an approximation for light intensity and detailed interactions/economics are marked HT/AQA depth unless explicitly taught.'

entries.subject: biology
entries.title: Uses of glucose
entries.summary: Trace the main uses of glucose made in photosynthesis.
entries.searchText: Uses of glucose Trace the main uses of glucose made in photosynthesis. ,must:['Glucose is used in respiration.','It can be converted to starch, cellulose and lipids/oils.','With nitrate ions it can be used to make amino acids and then proteins.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Development of the Periodic Table
entries.summary: Compare Newlands and Mendeleev and explain how evidence improved the model.
entries.searchText: Development of the Periodic Table Compare Newlands and Mendeleev and explain how evidence improved the model. ,must:['Mendeleev prioritised chemical properties, left gaps and made testable predictions.','Later discoveries matching predictions supported his arrangement.'],mistakes:['Do not say Mendeleev knew all the elements; leaving gaps was a strength.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
entries.summary: Distinguish the three using particles, bonding and separation.
entries.searchText: Elements, compounds and mixtures Distinguish the three using particles, bonding and separation. ,must:['Element: one type of atom.','Compound: elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions.','Mixture: substances together but not chemically bonded.'],mistakes:['A compound is not simply two substances mixed together.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Separation techniques
entries.summary: Choose filtration, crystallisation, evaporation or distillation from physical properties.
entries.searchText: Separation techniques Choose filtration, crystallisation, evaporation or distillation from physical properties. ,must:['Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.','Crystallisation can obtain a dissolved solid.','Distillation uses differences in boiling point.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Chromatography
entries.summary: Use chromatography to separate dissolved substances and interpret chromatograms.
entries.searchText: Chromatography Use chromatography to separate dissolved substances and interpret chromatograms. ,must:['Rf = distance travelled by substance ÷ distance travelled by solvent front.','Use the same baseline and solvent conditions when comparing results.'],practical:'Mark the baseline in pencil, place samples above the solvent level and measure distances from the baseline.'

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Atomic structure and isotopes
entries.summary: Use proton, neutron and electron properties to calculate atomic and mass numbers.
entries.searchText: Atomic structure and isotopes Use proton, neutron and electron properties to calculate atomic and mass numbers. ,must:['Atomic number = number of protons.','Mass number = protons + neutrons.','Isotopes have the same proton number but different neutron numbers.','For the first 20 elements, use the introductory shell model.'],mistakes:['Changing proton number changes the element.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Development of the atomic model
entries.summary: Link new experimental evidence to changes in scientific models.
entries.searchText: Development of the atomic model Link new experimental evidence to changes in scientific models. ,must:['sphere → plum pudding → nuclear model → Bohr shells → protons/neutrons','Alpha-scattering evidence supported a small dense positive nucleus and mostly empty space.','Peer review lets other scientists scrutinise methods, data and conclusions.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Formulae, conservation and balancing
entries.summary: Interpret formulae and balance symbol equations without changing substances.
entries.searchText: Formulae, conservation and balancing Interpret formulae and balance symbol equations without changing substances. ,must:['Mass is conserved in a closed system because atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.','Balance equations by changing coefficients, not formula subscripts.'],mistakes:['Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ does not “balance” water; it creates a different substance.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Crude oil, fractional distillation and alkanes
entries.summary: Explain how crude oil fractions are separated and recall alkane patterns.
entries.searchText: Crude oil, fractional distillation and alkanes Explain how crude oil fractions are separated and recall alkane patterns. ,must:['A hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen only.','Alkanes are saturated and follow CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.','First four: methane, ethane, propane, butane.','Longer chains generally have higher boiling points and viscosity and lower volatility/flammability.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Combustion and fossil-fuel pollution
entries.summary: Distinguish complete and incomplete combustion and explain key pollutants.
entries.searchText: Combustion and fossil-fuel pollution Distinguish complete and incomplete combustion and explain key pollutants. ,must:['Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms carbon dioxide and water.','Limited oxygen can produce carbon monoxide and/or soot.','Know impacts of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulates and carbon dioxide.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Cracking and alkenes
entries.summary: Explain why long hydrocarbons are cracked and recognise alkene chemistry.
entries.searchText: Cracking and alkenes Explain why long hydrocarbons are cracked and recognise alkene chemistry. ,must:['Cracking makes shorter alkanes and alkenes.','Alkenes are unsaturated, contain C=C and follow CₙH₂ₙ.','Bromine water changes from orange to colourless with an alkene.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Reactions of alkenes
entries.summary: Describe addition reactions across the C=C bond.
entries.searchText: Reactions of alkenes Describe addition reactions across the C=C bond. ,must:['Hydrogenation: alkene + hydrogen → alkane.','Hydration: alkene + steam → alcohol.','Halogenation adds halogen atoms across the double bond.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Addition polymerisation
entries.summary: Relate alkene monomers to long-chain addition polymers.
entries.searchText: Addition polymerisation Relate alkene monomers to long-chain addition polymers. ,must:['The C=C bond opens during addition polymerisation.','Many alkene monomers join to form a long saturated carbon chain.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Collision theory and reaction rates
entries.summary: Explain how concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts affect rate.
entries.searchText: Collision theory and reaction rates Explain how concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts affect rate. ,must:['Particles must collide with enough energy for a successful reaction.','Higher temperature increases kinetic energy and the fraction of collisions above activation energy.','A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up overall.']

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Rates practical and graph analysis
entries.summary: Plan, analyse and evaluate a rate experiment.
entries.searchText: Rates practical and graph analysis Plan, analyse and evaluate a rate experiment. ,must:['Steeper product-volume gradient means faster rate.','A plateau occurs when the limiting reactant is used up.','Instantaneous rate can be estimated from a tangent gradient.'],practical:'Required Practical 5: investigate concentration using a gas-volume method and/or a colour/turbidity endpoint; control relevant variables and repeat where useful.'

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.title: Greenhouse gases and climate change
entries.summary: Explain the greenhouse effect, human influences, carbon footprints and evidence.
entries.searchText: Greenhouse gases and climate change Explain the greenhouse effect, human influences, carbon footprints and evidence. ,must:['Important greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour.','Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.','Human activities can increase CO₂ and methane concentrations.','A carbon footprint covers greenhouse-gas emissions across a life cycle.'],mistakes:['The greenhouse effect is not ozone depletion.','Uncertainty in exact predictions does not mean there is no evidence.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Particle model of matter
entries.summary: Use particle arrangement and motion to explain solids, liquids and gases.
entries.searchText: Particle model of matter Use particle arrangement and motion to explain solids, liquids and gases. ,must:['Solid particles are close and vibrate about fixed positions.','Liquid particles are close but can move past each other.','Gas particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions.','Temperature relates to average particle kinetic energy.'],mistakes:['Particles do not simply expand when a substance is heated.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Density
entries.summary: Use density calculations and methods for regular solids, irregular solids and liquids.
entries.searchText: Density Use density calculations and methods for regular solids, irregular solids and liquids. ,must:['ρ = m ÷ V','Use consistent units; SI density is kg/m³.'],practical:'Required Practical 5: measure mass and volume appropriately; use water displacement for irregular solids and subtract container mass for liquids.'

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Internal energy and heating
entries.summary: Distinguish temperature from total internal energy.
entries.searchText: Internal energy and heating Distinguish temperature from total internal energy. ,must:['Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a system.','Heating may raise particle kinetic energy/temperature or change particle potential energy during a state change.'],mistakes:['Internal energy is not simply “heat inside an object”.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Conduction and thermal insulation
entries.summary: Explain energy transfer in solids and evaluate insulation.
entries.searchText: Conduction and thermal insulation Explain energy transfer in solids and evaluate insulation. ,must:['Vibrating particles transfer energy to neighbours.','Free electrons help metals conduct thermal energy rapidly.','Trapped gases can reduce conduction and bulk movement.'],practical:'Required Practical 2: compare insulating materials under controlled conditions using equal starting conditions, timing and measurements.'

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Infrared radiation and surfaces
entries.summary: Compare absorption, emission and reflection of infrared radiation.
entries.searchText: Infrared radiation and surfaces Compare absorption, emission and reflection of infrared radiation. ,must:['Hotter objects generally emit infrared at a greater rate.','Dark matt surfaces are good absorbers/emitters; light shiny surfaces are poorer absorbers/emitters and better reflectors.'],practical:'A Leslie cube demonstration compares infrared emitted by surfaces with different finishes.',extension:'Do not relabel the TGS classroom Leslie-cube demonstration as a separate Year 9 required practical unless the teacher does so.'

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Specific heat capacity
entries.summary: Use ΔE = mcΔθ and understand the required practical.
entries.searchText: Specific heat capacity Use ΔE = mcΔθ and understand the required practical. ,must:['Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1°C.','ΔE = m c Δθ','Use temperature change, not final temperature.'],practical:'Required Practical 1: measure block mass, energy supplied and temperature rise, reduce heat loss and calculate c; repeated readings/graphs can strengthen evidence.'

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Changes of state
entries.summary: Explain melting, freezing, boiling/evaporation and condensation using particles and heating curves.
entries.searchText: Changes of state Explain melting, freezing, boiling/evaporation and condensation using particles and heating curves. ,must:['Changes of state are physical and reversible.','During a phase change of a pure substance at constant pressure, energy can transfer while temperature stays constant.','Flat graph sections show state changes.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Power and energy
entries.summary: Use power to describe the rate of energy transfer or work done.
entries.searchText: Power and energy Use power to describe the rate of energy transfer or work done. ,must:['P = E ÷ t','P = W ÷ t','1 watt = 1 joule per second.'],mistakes:['Power is a rate; it is not the same quantity as energy.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Specific latent heat
entries.summary: Calculate energy for a change of state at constant temperature.
entries.searchText: Specific latent heat Calculate energy for a change of state at constant temperature. ,must:['E = mL','Fusion is solid ↔ liquid; vaporisation is liquid ↔ gas.','Specific latent heat changes state without changing temperature.'],mistakes:['Do not use ΔE=mcΔθ for the flat phase-change section.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Evaporation
entries.summary: Use particle energy to explain evaporation and cooling.
entries.searchText: Evaporation Use particle energy to explain evaporation and cooling. ,must:['Evaporation occurs at a liquid surface and can occur below boiling point.','Higher-energy particles are more likely to escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left.','Higher temperature, larger surface area, greater air movement and lower humidity increase evaporation.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Gas pressure and temperature
entries.summary: Explain why pressure rises with temperature at constant volume.
entries.searchText: Gas pressure and temperature Explain why pressure rises with temperature at constant volume. ,must:['Higher temperature means greater average particle kinetic energy.','Particles collide with walls more frequently and with greater momentum change.'],mistakes:['Pressure–volume work assumes constant temperature; this pressure–temperature explanation assumes constant volume.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Energy stores and pathways
entries.summary: Describe energy stores, transfers, conservation and dissipation.
entries.searchText: Energy stores and pathways Describe energy stores, transfers, conservation and dissipation. ,must:['Stores include kinetic, thermal/internal, gravitational, elastic, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear.','Transfers can be mechanical, electrical, by heating or by radiation.','Energy is conserved but may become dissipated.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Kinetic energy
entries.summary: Calculate and reason with kinetic energy.
entries.searchText: Kinetic energy Calculate and reason with kinetic energy. ,must:['Eₖ = ½mv²','Doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times larger if mass is unchanged.'],mistakes:['Square the speed, not the mass.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Gravitational potential energy
entries.summary: Calculate GPE and explain transfers between GPE, kinetic and dissipated stores.
entries.searchText: Gravitational potential energy Calculate GPE and explain transfers between GPE, kinetic and dissipated stores. ,must:['Eₚ = mgh','As an object falls, gravitational energy can transfer to kinetic energy; resistance may dissipate some energy.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Elastic potential energy
entries.summary: Calculate energy stored in a spring and interpret the graph area.
entries.searchText: Elastic potential energy Calculate energy stored in a spring and interpret the graph area. ,must:['Eₑ = ½ke² below the limit of proportionality.','For a linear force–extension graph, area under the graph gives work done/energy transferred.'],mistakes:['Extension must be in metres for standard SI calculations.']

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Efficiency
entries.summary: Calculate efficiency and explain how unwanted transfers can be reduced.
entries.searchText: Efficiency Calculate efficiency and explain how unwanted transfers can be reduced. ,must:['efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input','or useful power output ÷ total power input','Efficiency is between 0 and 1, or 0% and 100%.','Reduce specific unwanted transfers through design, insulation or reduced friction where relevant.']
